Construct tensors from the two NumPy arrays, explicitly convert each to its declared dtype, and inspect the resulting shapes and dtypes. Return the aligned pair as a tuple only after checking the common batch length and required axes. Keeping these checks separate makes it clear whether a failure concerns feature shape, target shape, dtype or matching observations, rather than reporting only that conversion succeeded.

Inspect features and targets separately before checking their common observation axis. A classification target representation may differ from numerical features, so an explicit cast should use the target's declared dtype rather than a shared convenience setting. Return the pair only after the axes and representations satisfy the contract. In the three-target failure fixture, tensor conversion may still succeed; the alignment check is what rejects it. teaching_blocks.content:

Finally, compare the model output with the declared target/loss contract. The architecture example remains bounded to that contract rather than adding layers or final nonlinearities simply because they appear in another task.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Take X=[[1, 2], [3, 4]] and the supplied derivative D=[[0.1], [0.2]] for Z=XW+b. The weight-gradient reference is X.T @ D = [[0.7], [1.0]], and the bias-gradient reference is [0.3]. Any loss reduction is already included in D; dividing again would change the reference. Set trainable leaf tensors to require gradients, form the scalar loss and call backward. Inspect .grad before clearing it, and compare shapes and values under explicit tolerances. For a fresh computation, clear the old gradients first because backward accumulates. Include a failure fixture whose gradient differs from the declared reference, not only a successful call.

Read the matrix reference one parameter at a time. The first weight combines feature values 1 and 3 with derivatives 0.1 and 0.2, giving 0.7. The second combines 2 and 4 with the same derivatives, giving 1.0. The bias combines derivatives over rows, giving 0.3. These shapes are part of the check: a transpose error can yield a different object even when some scalar values look plausible. Because D includes the loss reduction, use it once as supplied. Compare after backward and before clearing so the inspected gradients correspond to the intended fresh computation rather than zeroed or accumulated state.

teaching_blocks.content: Backward does not overwrite every old gradient automatically. A gradient comparison also needs the correct matrix shapes and reduction convention; a numerically plausible scalar is not the weight matrix reference.

media.group_title: How autograd carries derivatives through a computation graph

segments.label: Trace a scalar tensor computation and inspect its gradient
segments.summary: PyTorch tracks operations on a tensor when requires_grad=True. Starting with a three-element tensor x, the demonstration forms y = x + 2, multiplies y by itself and by 2, and takes the mean to produce a scalar. Each tracked operation contributes to a computation graph and has an associated gradient function. Calling backward() on the scalar computes its derivative with respect to x and stores the result in x.grad. Repeating the construction without enabling gradient tracking leads to an error when backward() is called. The explanation connects differentiation through the graph to the chain rule: local derivatives are combined to obtain the final gradient. Because the output is scalar, this backward() call needs no explicit gradient argument.

coverage.learning_objective: Choose a task-compatible loss and verify its output, target and gradient contracts.

required_facts.statement: A loss compares model outputs with the corresponding target representation; choose its input contract before computing the scalar objective.
source_refs: pytorch_learn_basics#optimization_tutorial.html — Hyperparameters; Loss Function; Optimizer; Full Implementation

required_facts.statement: CrossEntropyLoss expects unnormalized class logits; for class-index targets, logits have shape (N, C), targets have shape (N,) with dtype long and values in [0, C).
MSELoss takes input and target tensors of the same shape and, under mean reduction, averages their squared elementwise differences.
BCEWithLogitsLoss combines sigmoid and binary cross-entropy for logits and same-shaped targets in [0, 1], rather than expecting already-sigmoid-transformed inputs.

For mean squared error over M output elements, the loss derivative with respect to an output is 2 × (output−target)/M, so its sign points toward increasing loss as the output moves away from the target.
For unweighted mean binary cross-entropy with logits over M elements, the logit derivative is (sigmoid(logit)−target)/M; this distinguishes the probability representation from the raw logit.

For mean class-index cross-entropy without weighting, the derivative per sample logit is (softmax probability−one-hot target)/N, so output width, target identity and reduction affect the gradient reference.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For an unweighted mean squared-error fixture with outputs [2, 4] and targets [1, 2], the loss is (1²+2²)/2 = 2.5 and output derivatives are [1, 2]. For a binary-logit fixture with one logit 0 and target 1, sigmoid(0)=0.5, so the supplied mean-logit derivative is −0.5. For target 1, decreasing the logit increases loss, while increasing it decreases loss. For a class-index task with three classes, verify logits width 3 and long target indices in [0, 3); use the stated softmax-minus-one-hot reference with its sample-count reduction. These are distinct output contracts, not interchangeable wrappers around arbitrary tensors.

Keep the mean-reduction factor visible in each reference. The two-element MSE fixture divides squared errors by two, while the one-element binary-logit fixture divides its sigmoid-minus-target derivative by one. A class-index cross-entropy reference subtracts the one-hot target from the softmax vector and divides by the sample count. Those equations support different target representations, so verify target dtype and axes before applying them. A positive-looking scalar loss is not proof of the right contract. Compare both value and derivative direction in the bounded fixture, retaining the supplied assumptions about unweighted mean reduction.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: CrossEntropyLoss expects unnormalized logits for the class-index case; BCEWithLogitsLoss also expects logits, not already-sigmoid inputs. MSE's same-shape contract must be checked rather than left to accidental broadcasting.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose minimized validation values are 0.50, 0.44, 0.43 and 0.45, with min_delta 0.02 and patience 2. The move from 0.50 to 0.44 is sufficient improvement and resets the counter. The value 0.43 does not satisfy 0.43 < 0.44−0.02, so the counter becomes one; 0.45 makes it two and exhausts patience. The lowest observed value is 0.43, but the best checkpoint accepted under min_delta is the one at 0.44. Retain the 0.44 checkpoint’s weights, preserving them by deep copy or a saved state file. Bound the while loop by maximum epochs as well as the non-improvement rule. Protected-test observations do not decide patience or checkpoint choice.

Inspect CPU and memory measurements and running process state during the profiled interval, using docker stats and docker top for a containerized run, to distinguish resource limits from stage timing evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Warm up the bounded workload, then profile its labeled regions. If the trace attributes most measured work to loading, test one supported loading factor rather than immediately changing model computation. Inspect CPU, memory and process state during the same interval; for the container fixture, docker stats and docker top provide that supporting evidence. After the change, compare the same bounded workload again without profiler overhead in the final timing. On CUDA, synchronize measurement boundaries so a CPU clock includes completed accelerator work. Keep the profiling attribution separate from the final unprofiled performance comparison, since they answer related but different questions.

The profiler trace supplies attribution, while the unprofiled rerun supplies the matched elapsed-time comparison. Keep the same bounded workload and one-factor change between those two comparisons. A loading-region label should enclose the intended loading work; a model-compute label should identify that separate work rather than blend it with setup. Runtime CPU, memory and process evidence must refer to the same window. Synchronization at accelerator timing boundaries accounts for asynchronous completion. This makes the observed difference interpretable without assuming that a profiler's overhead or a shifted measurement boundary is a genuine speed improvement.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A code change is not evidence of improvement. Asynchronous accelerator work and profiler overhead can alter timing interpretation unless the measurement boundaries and final comparison are controlled.
